name: The Test Scheduler
oneLiner: Load-balances a feature's test cases across the team by weighted priority and emits a phased schedule as Word and Excel deliverables.
lead: Automates test-execution planning: pulls live test-case counts from ADO, distributes stories across the team so no one is overloaded, lays a phased timeline on business days, assesses risk, and renders stakeholder-ready Word and Excel documents. Removes the half-day of manual spreadsheet math a lead does every sprint.
chore: Before every sprint a lead builds the plan by hand: count each story's test cases, estimate capacity, assign urgent stories to the right people, sketch a timeline, enumerate risks, and format it into something management will read. It takes half a day, the weighting math is error-prone, and one tester silently ends up overloaded.
instead: Give it the feature ID, the team roster, and the sprint dates. It reads the real test-case counts, balances load by weighted priority (P1 counts 1.5x, P4 only 0.3x), builds a phased timeline with milestones on business days, runs rule-based risk checks, and writes the Test Plan and Execution Schedule as Word and Excel — no hand-formatting.
whyItMatters: A weighted, business-day-accurate schedule is the difference between a sprint that lands on time and one where the busiest tester becomes a silent bottleneck.

howItWorks.step: Reads the feature and its stories from ADO and counts the test cases linked to each.
howItWorks.explain: Builds the `{ feature, stories }` snapshot the whole plan is computed from — counts are read live, never cached. Every title falls back to a synthetic `Feature #id` / `Story #id` so a blank ADO field never surfaces as `undefined` downstream. The `storyIds.sort((a, b) => a - b)` is a **numeric** sort on purpose — JavaScript's default sort is lexicographic, which would order `10` before `2` — giving deterministic story order. `priority` defaults to `2` (mid-range) when unset so an unprioritised story pulls neither the heaviest nor lightest weight later, and `testCaseCount` is simply the number of `TestedBy-Forward` relations — that integer, not the test content, is the load unit the balancer divides across the team.

howItWorks.step: Distributes stories across the team by weighted load — high-priority stories weigh more so no one is overloaded.
howItWorks.explain: A greedy load balancer that packs the biggest items first. It sorts by `a.priority - b.priority` (lower number = more urgent, so P1 leads) and tie-breaks on `b.testCaseCount - a.testCaseCount` (heaviest story first) — assigning large items first is what keeps a greedy fill from stranding a big story on an already-full member at the end. For each story it picks the `target` with the **lowest `weightedLoad`** via `reduce`, not the lowest raw count, so a member holding one heavy P1 isn't handed more work than someone with several trivial P4s. `weight` comes from `PRIORITY_WEIGHTS[story.priority] ?? 1.0` — the `?? 1.0` guards an unrecognised priority from producing `NaN` and poisoning every later comparison. `weightedLoad` accumulates `count * weight` to steer assignment while `totalTCs` keeps the honest raw count for the schedule.

howItWorks.step: Splits the sprint into three phases — TC creation, execution, bug triage/retest — over business days only.
howItWorks.explain: Phase sizing is fixed-priority, not proportional: execution and triage are each **capped at 4 business days** (`Math.min(4, ...)`) and creation absorbs whatever is left, because a longer sprint benefits from more prep time, not a longer execution window. The `totalDays - 2` when sizing execution reserves a minimum sliver for the other two phases, and `Math.max(1, ...)` on `creationDays` guarantees at least one creation day even when a short sprint would otherwise compute zero or negative. Dates are then laid down sequentially with `addBusinessDays`, always stepping `+1` between phases so the next phase opens on the following working day rather than doubling up on the prior phase's end date — and every hop skips weekends because it counts business days, not calendar days.

howItWorks.step: Derives milestones — kickoff, 50% checkpoint, sign-off — each with a date and owner.
howItWorks.explain: Milestones are derived, not stored — each one reads straight off a phase boundary in `timeline.phases`, so they can never drift out of sync with the schedule. Kickoff and completion of creation map to `phases[0]`'s start/end, execution start/complete to `phases[1]`, and sign-off to `phases[2]`'s end. The only computed date is the `50% Checkpoint`: `addBusinessDays(phases[1].startDate, Math.floor(phases[1].businessDays / 2))` lands it on the midpoint working day of the execution phase, `Math.floor` biasing it slightly early on odd-length phases. Every milestone is stamped `owner: leadName` and `status: 'Pending'` so the emitted plan is a ready-to-track checklist rather than just dates.

howItWorks.step: Runs rule-based risk checks — TCs-per-person over threshold, too-short sprint, uneven load — each with a mitigation.
howItWorks.explain: Threshold rules, not model inference — each tripped rule appends a typed risk with a fixed `id`, `category`, `severity`, and a concrete `mitigation`, so the same plan always flags the same risks. `tcsPerPerson` averages total test cases over head-count, guarded by `team.length > 0 ? ... : 0` so an empty roster yields `0` rather than a `NaN` that would silently bypass the `> 50` overload check (R-1). The schedule rule (R-2) fires under 10 business days but grades its own severity — `totalBusinessDays < 7 ? 'High' : 'Medium'` — so a genuinely crushed timeline is escalated while a merely tight one is a warning. Both descriptions interpolate the actual numbers (`Math.round(tcsPerPerson)`, the day count) so the risk reads as specific evidence, not a generic label.

howItWorks.step: Serializes the plan to JSON, Markdown, Excel, and — with `--word` — two formatted Word documents.
howItWorks.explain: One computed `planData` fans out to every format so consumers pick their own — nothing is recomputed per file. JSON goes through `planToJson` and is pretty-printed at 2-space for machine hand-off; Markdown and the per-member xlsx are always written. Every filename embeds `${input.featureId}` and a `${ts}` timestamp, so re-running never clobbers a prior plan — each run is a distinct dated artifact (this agent has no fingerprinting, by design). The two Word documents are gated behind `if (input.generateWord)` because docx rendering is the most expensive step and only matters when a stakeholder-facing deliverable is actually requested.

examples.caption: A two-week sprint for a four-person team
examples.input: A feature with 12 stories totalling 90 test cases, a team of 4, sprint dates 1–14.
examples.output: A balanced slice per tester (~22 TCs each), a timeline with a 4-day execution window, a 50% checkpoint milestone, and a risk flag: 'Moderate load — 22 TCs per person; monitor from Day 3.' Delivered as Word and Excel.

examples.caption: A sprint that's too tight
examples.input: A feature with 60 test cases, a team of 2, only 6 business days.
examples.output: A high-severity schedule risk (R-2): 'Short sprint — only 6 business days. Prioritize P1/P2 stories; defer P3,' alongside the balanced per-person schedule.

underHood.heading: Reads the feature and counts test cases
underHood.whenRuns: First, on the feature ID you pass.
underHood.output: Every story under the feature, its priority, and its linked test-case count, via the ADO REST API.

underHood.heading: Balances the workload
underHood.whenRuns: Once, right after the stories are counted.
underHood.input: The story list and the team roster.
underHood.output: Each member's assigned stories, weighted so P1 work counts 1.5x standard and P4 only 0.3x.

underHood.heading: Builds the sprint timeline
underHood.whenRuns: Once, from the sprint's start and end dates.
underHood.input: The sprint start and end dates.
underHood.output: Three phases — TC creation, execution, bug triage — each sized in business days.

underHood.heading: Assesses risk
underHood.whenRuns: After workload and timeline are both set.
underHood.input: Per-person load, sprint length, and story distribution.
underHood.output: A typed list of risks — overload, too-short sprint, uneven distribution — each with a mitigation.

underHood.heading: Produces the deliverables
underHood.input: The computed plan, schedule, milestones, and risks.
underHood.output: JSON and Markdown, an xlsx workbook with one sheet per member, and — with `--word` — a Test Plan and a Test Execution Plan docx.

prerequisites: Node ≥ 18 and a terminal (macOS/Linux shell or Windows PowerShell).
Read access to Azure DevOps and a **personal access token** (`ADO_PAT`).
The feature's stories must already have test cases linked (the Test-Plan Author produces these) — counts are pulled live.
The team roster and the sprint's start/end dates.

steps.label: Install Node.js — the runtime for the agent.
steps.cmd:
# macOS (with Homebrew):
brew install node

# or download the LTS installer from nodejs.org, then check it worked:
node -v   # should print v18 or higher
steps.why: The agent is a TypeScript program executed under Node. One-time install per machine.
steps.firstRun: First time on a new machine only.

steps.label: Clone the code and install dependencies.
steps.why: `npm install` resolves the agent's dependencies — the ADO REST client and the docx/xlsx writers — into `node_modules`.
steps.rerun: No-op unless the dependency set changed.

steps.label: Set the environment variables.
steps.cmd:
export ADO_ORGANIZATION=my-org
export ADO_PROJECT="My Project"
export ADO_PAT=your-access-token
steps.why: Read at startup: the ADO org/project to query and the PAT that authorizes it. No LLM key needed — this agent is deterministic scheduling math, no model calls.

steps.label: Dry-run first — print the numbers without writing files.
steps.cmd:
npx ts-node agents/test-execution-planner-agent.ts \
  --feature-id 5001 \
  --team "Alex P|Jordan K|Sam R|Taylor M" \
  --sprint Sprint-12 \
  --start-date 2026-08-03 --end-date 2026-08-14 \
  --dry-run
steps.why: `--team` is a pipe-separated roster; `--dry-run` prints story count, total test cases, and team size to stdout without writing files — a sanity check before the real run.

steps.label: Run for real; add `--word` for the formatted documents.
steps.cmd:
npx ts-node agents/test-execution-planner-agent.ts \
  --feature-id 5001 \
  --team "Alex P|Jordan K|Sam R|Taylor M" \
  --sprint Sprint-12 \
  --start-date 2026-08-03 --end-date 2026-08-14 \
  --word
steps.why: Drop `--dry-run`, add `--word`. Writes the balanced schedule, timeline, risks, and milestones to disk, plus a Test Plan and a Test Execution Plan docx.
steps.firstRun: Computes the full schedule and writes every file.
steps.rerun: No fingerprinting — recomputes fresh. Re-run whenever the team, dates, or story list change.

steps.label: Open the results.
steps.why: JSON, Markdown, an xlsx workbook (one sheet per member), and — with `--word` — the two docx files, all in one folder.

inputs.name: --feature-id <id>
inputs.desc: The feature to schedule — its stories and linked test-case counts are pulled live from ADO.

inputs.name: --team "Name1|Name2|..."
inputs.desc: Pipe-separated roster to balance the load across.

inputs.name: --sprint <name> --start-date <date> --end-date <date>
inputs.desc: The sprint label and its calendar start/end dates, used to size the phased timeline in business days.

inputs.name: --word / --dry-run
inputs.desc: --word also emits the Word documents; --dry-run prints the summary and writes nothing.

outputs.name: ExecutionPlan_<id>_<timestamp>.json / .md
outputs.desc: The full computed plan — weighted workload, timeline, milestones, risks — machine- and human-readable.

outputs.name: ExecutionSchedule_<id>_<timestamp>.xlsx
outputs.desc: An xlsx workbook with a sheet per team member plus a combined assignments view.

outputs.name: TestPlan_<id>_<timestamp>.docx / TestExecutionPlan_<id>_<timestamp>.docx
outputs.desc: Two Word documents (only with --word) — a stakeholder-ready Test Plan and a day-by-day Test Execution Plan.

runbook.rerun: No fingerprinting — every run recomputes the schedule from the feature's current story and test-case counts. Re-run whenever the roster, sprint dates, or story list change; each run gets a fresh timestamp so nothing is overwritten.
runbook.integrate: Consumes the test-case counts the **Test-Plan Author** produced. Run at sprint planning and again on any mid-sprint scope shift — the risk flags (overload, short sprint, uneven distribution) are worth re-checking each time.

video.caption: A 3-4 minute screen recording: pass a feature ID and a roster, and watch the weighted schedule and Word documents land.
script: Open a terminal; have the feature's ticket open in a browser tab for reference.
Say: 'This agent decides who tests what, by when — and writes it up as a real document.'
Run `node -v` to confirm Node is installed; one line on what Node is.
Run `npm install` (or note it's done); explain it grabs the helper libraries.
Show the `export` lines; say this is the only client-specific part — no AI key needed here.
Run the command with `--dry-run`; point out the story count, total test cases, and team size it prints.
Re-run without `--dry-run`, adding `--word`; narrate as it balances load and builds the timeline.
Open the Excel file; click through two team members' sheets to show the balance.
Open the Test Plan Word doc; scroll to the risk-assessment table.
Point at one risk row — e.g. 'short sprint' — and read its suggested mitigation.
Close: 'That's a stakeholder-ready plan, built in under a minute.'
